## Overview

Report successful NIXL pulls before the next model output so the decoder can admit requests sooner. Set `"enable_early_recv": true` in the decoder's `--kv-transfer-config`; disabled by default.

## Claims

Supports `uni` and single-node `mp`, TP, sync/async scheduling, and NIXL pull inside MultiConnector; decoder PP=1. Existing threads perform polling. Successful receives share the normal all-worker quorum; transfer failures retain normal recovery.

## Validation

Head `49c901449`, base `df028dffa`. Since `053f5967e`, workers spin between polls instead of sleeping. In a CPU-only probe with a no-op poll, an RPC that arrives while a pull is pending is picked up 3–15 µs later than on main at p50 (sleep: ~150 µs later), with the same waiting-thread CPU as main. **20 focused tests passed**, covering quorum, failure deferral, NIXL one-shot reporting, scheduler admission/abort, and terminal polling errors. Five local negative controls confirmed that the shortened tests reject premature completion, lost failure votes, missing lifecycle updates, and nonterminal exceptions. Changed-file pre-commit including mypy passed; source hashes match validation.

```bash
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' \
uv run --no-project .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \
  tests/v1/executor/test_early_kv_recv.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_remote_prefill_lifecycle.py::test_basic_lifecycle \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_remote_prefill_lifecycle.py::test_kv_fetch_stages_cleared_on_abort \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py::test_early_recv_reports_successes_only_through_poll \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py::test_early_recv_leaves_failures_to_the_step \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_output_aggregator.py
```

Dedicated IPC/idle-loop tests were removed to keep the regression suite focused. Earlier `860085f7a` Qwen3-0.6B NIXL P/D, TP2 + MultiConnector, mp/async off/on checks returned identical 32-token outputs for 32 requests. On H200 with Qwen3-8B TP1 (NIXL pull, `mp`, 96 background decode streams, one 4K-token handoff per second, 240 handoffs per arm), median decoder first-token latency on this head was 97.2 ms vs 106.1 ms on main with async scheduling (vLLM's default here, −8.4%) and 93.2 ms vs 93.9 ms with sync; background ITL p50 stayed within 0.1 ms of main and worker CPU matched main. Uni serving/fault recovery, stalled TP8 performance, ROCm/Mamba and heterogeneous layouts remain validation gaps. Upstream CI is separate.

## Details

Completion flows from worker post-processing through IPC/quorum counting to the existing scheduler lifecycle. Known-failed early votes use the normal output replay queue; no extra ready-failure set or aggregate override is needed. The public aggregator is unchanged. Each worker reports a load once; no speculative rank/load deduplication is added. Unexpected MP poll/channel errors terminate the worker and use its existing monitor, including while paused; uni marks polling errors terminal.

Disabled mode retains the ordinary aggregator and scheduling paths, with added flag checks/forwarding calls. Between RPCs, workers spin with `sched_yield` like `MessageQueue.dequeue()` and poll every 0.2 ms while pulls are pending; an RPC that arrives during a poll waits for it. Post-processing uses the current worker stream; metrics still use ordinary outputs. KV pressure can delay admission.

#51919 uses additional notification threads; this implementation reuses existing threads. AI assistance was used for implementation and validation.

Hi, thanks for working on this!

I hit the same issue with **MooncakeStoreConnector + pipeline parallelism prefill**: when a KV load finishes, the scheduler only gets notified a few steps later, and the delay grows with the PP size. Your early-receive path fixes this nicely, and I've added Mooncake Store support on top of it with a small change:

- implement `has_pending_recving()` / `poll_finished_recving()` for MooncakeStoreConnector, so successful Mooncake Store loads are reported early;
- keep failed loads on the existing `get_finished()` path. They are not reported early, so the scheduler always sees the failure before it would run the request;
- drop the `PP == 1` check from the generic config validation. NIXL still rejects PP on its own, so nothing changes for NIXL.

Commit (on top of your latest head): [xsxszab/vllm@bba3ce6](https://github.com/xsxszab/vllm/commit/bba3ce6398)

---
**Setup:** Qwen3-32B on a single B300 node, TP=1, async scheduling, Mooncake Store over RDMA.

**Workload:** two kinds of requests run at the same time:

- **Measured requests** (2 req/s): each reuses an 8K-token prefix that is already stored in Mooncake, so vLLM loads that prefix from Mooncake and only computes the 128 new tokens.
- **Background requests:** random prompts with no shared prefix, so they never touch Mooncake. They only keep the GPUs busy. The "Background load" column below gives their prompt length and rate.

The table shows the TTFT of the measured requests only, with early receive off → on:

| PP | Background load | TTFT p50 | TTFT p90 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1K-token prompts, 4 req/s | 179 → 151 ms | 246 → 213 ms |
| 1 | 2K-token prompts, 6 req/s | 352 → 285 ms | 723 → 591 ms |
| 2 | 1K-token prompts, 4 req/s | 145 → 127 ms | 203 → 181 ms |
| 2 | 2K-token prompts, 6 req/s | 223 → 200 ms | 441 → 374 ms |
| 4 | 1K-token prompts, 4 req/s | 110 → 100 ms | 149 → 141 ms |
| 4 | 2K-token prompts, 6 req/s | 165 → 148 ms | 329 → 296 ms |
| 4 | 3K-token prompts, 6 req/s | 367 → 305 ms | 1242 → 941 ms |

Each row pools 2–3 runs per setting (~450 requests, ~200 for the last row). These numbers were measured on your earlier head (`47fb7e3`, before the switch to sleep-based waiting). I'm still re-running them on the current head and will post an update later.

---

One thing I noticed: the worker polling between RPCs matters a lot under heavy load. With it turned off, most of the gain was gone near saturation.

Related to that, polling may not be the best fit for every connector. Mooncake Store loads run in their own recv threads, which already know exactly when a load finishes, so they could push the notification right away instead of waiting for the worker to poll. An optional push-style hook (for example, a thread-safe notify function that a connector can call from its own thread) would keep the same benefit without the polling cost or the up-to-0.2 ms delay before the worker picks up the next RPC. I'm not asking to add it to this PR; I'm still trying to prototype it on my side to see if it works, just mention it here for completeness.

I can open this as a follow-up PR once this one is merged, and keep it rebased on your branch until then. If you'd rather have it land together with this PR, I can open a PR against your branch instead.

Small idea to simplify the worker loop: could we combine waiting for the next RPC with waiting for the next poll?

At the top of each iteration, run the poll if it is due; otherwise wait for an RPC, but only until the next poll is due. This replaces both `wait_for_poll()` and the post-step poll.

```python
rpc_mq = self.rpc_broadcast_mq
early_kv_recv = self.early_kv_recv

while True:
    if early_kv_recv is not None:
        timeout = early_kv_recv.time_until_poll()  # None: nothing to poll for
        if timeout is not None:
            if timeout <= 0:
                get_watch_dog().feed()
                early_kv_recv.poll()
                continue
            with get_watch_dog().disable():
                if not early_kv_recv.wait_for_rpc(rpc_mq, timeout):
                    continue

    with get_watch_dog().disable():
        rpc_request = rpc_mq.dequeue(indefinite=True)
    self._execute_worker_rpc(rpc_request)

    if early_kv_recv is not None and rpc_request[0] in (
        "execute_model",
        "sample_tokens",
    ):
        early_kv_recv.step_rpc_done()
    del rpc_request
```

This needs two new `EarlyKVRecvSender` methods in place of `wait_for_poll()`:

- `time_until_poll()` returns the seconds until `_next_poll`, or `None` when no poll is needed.
- `wait_for_rpc(rpc_mq, timeout)` spins on `rpc_mq.readable()` with `sched_yield()` for up to `timeout` seconds. It returns `True` once an RPC is ready or the queue is shutting down, and returns `False` when the poll is due.
- `step_rpc_done()` would also set `_next_poll = 0.0`, making the poll due at the top of the next iteration. This preserves immediate post-step polling without a separate call after the step or any assumption about the RPC duration.

Happy to prototype this and compare CPU usage and latency if the direction looks useful.

@xsxszab Thanks for the measurements and the Mooncake Store patch.

**Waiting:** you were right about spinning. The sleep came from our `85e8fef3f`, where we only compared CPU against the earlier spin; `MessageQueue.dequeue()` on main already spins with `sched_yield` for 1 s after each read, so the sleep saved CPU only relative to an idle worker and delayed RPCs that arrived during the wait by ~150 µs. `49c901449` spins on `readable()` with `sched_yield` until the next poll, like `dequeue()`. In a CPU-only probe with a no-op poll, an RPC that arrives while a pull is pending is now picked up 3–15 µs later than on main at p50, with the same CPU as main. Your `47fb7e3` numbers used the same kind of wait; a rerun on `49c901449` would confirm them.

**Loop restructure:** with the spin in `wait_for_poll()`, we'd keep the current loop. Setting `_next_poll = 0` in `step_rpc_done()` would make the sync output rank poll twice (it already polls in `enqueue_output()` after `get_output()`), and it adds two methods without changing behavior.

**Mooncake Store:** happy to include it in this PR. I've invited you as a collaborator on `Sy0307/vllm`. Once you accept, please push the Mooncake commit (not the `[Experiment]` ones) to `perf/kv-early-recv-multirank-fix` on top of `49c901449` as a separate commit, without force-pushing, so it can be split out if reviewers ask. Before that:

1. NIXL only rejects PP>1 for `kv_role == "kv_consumer"`; `kv_both` with PP>1 still gets through. If the generic `PP == 1` check goes, please reject `enable_early_recv` with PP>1 on the NIXL side so NIXL support is unchanged.
2. An early-off/on output comparison with PP=2 (greedy, ideally `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, with requests completing through early receive). The quorum has only been checked with TP so far.
3. `_report_load_error()` and `get_and_clear_finished_requests()` now track load errors even with early receive off. Please gate that on `enable_early_recv` so the disabled path matches main.
4. `has_pending_recving()` could assert `connector_worker`, like the NIXL hook.
5. Updated TTFT on the new head (PP 1/2/4). Post them here and I'll add the Mooncake/PP scope and results to the PR description.

Agreed on the push-style hook as a separate prototype.

H200 GPU check of the spin change (`49c901449`) against main (`df028dffa`, this PR's base) and the previous sleep-based head (`053f5967e`).

Setup: Qwen3-8B, TP1, one H200 each for the prefiller and the decoder, NIXL pull, `mp` executor, CUDA graphs. The prefiller runs main in every arm. The decoder serves 96 background decode streams while one 4K-token handoff arrives per second. Two runs per arm, 120 handoffs per run, ordered main → sleep → spin → spin → sleep → main. Latency is measured from the decoder request to its first streamed token, so prefill is excluded. Every handoff in the early arms (240 per arm) completed through early receive. Async scheduling is vLLM's default for this setup; the sync rows use `--no-async-scheduling`.

| Decoder first token, p50 (240 handoffs) | main | sleep (`053f5967e`) | spin (`49c901449`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| async scheduling | 106.1 ms | 102.4 ms (−3.5%) | 97.2 ms (−8.4%) |
| sync scheduling | 93.9 ms | 96.2 ms (+2.4%) | 93.2 ms (−0.7%) |

- Per-run p50: async main 106.4 / 105.6, sleep 101.6 / 103.8, spin 93.4 / 100.5 ms; sync main 96.6 / 91.4, sleep 96.2 / 96.2, spin 92.3 / 94.1 ms.
- Background ITL p50 per run: async main 13.59 / 13.60, sleep 13.64 / 13.61, spin 13.59 / 13.59 ms; sync main 15.91 / 15.86, sleep 15.97 / 15.94, spin 15.94 / 15.94 ms.
- Decoder worker-process CPU: async 2.07–2.08 cores for main and spin, 2.09 for sleep; sync 1.31 for main, 1.31–1.32 for spin, 1.33–1.34 for sleep.

Takeaways:

- With async scheduling, the spin head lowers median decoder first-token latency by 8.4% versus main, with the same ITL and worker CPU.
- With sync scheduling, the median is unchanged and ITL p50 is about 0.05 ms (0.3%) higher.
- Spin was below sleep in each run pair, but with two runs per arm the 3–5 ms gap is within run-to-run spread, so I don't attribute it to the wait change alone.
- Means and p90 swing between runs (for example, main async p90 is 1287 / 805 ms), so I'm not drawing conclusions from them.

Thanks! I pushed Mooncake Store support and a small docs follow-up.

Output correctness, TTFT gain, and load-failure handling have been tested, including P/D with `MultiConnector`, and the results look good.

> One clarification: `NIXLConnector` (pull) does not support PP, while `MooncakeStoreConnector` does. The results below validate early receive with PP prefill and MooncakeStoreConnector. The full PD setup—`MultiConnector[NIXLConnector, MooncakeStoreConnector]` on the prefill side and `NIXLConnector` on the decode side—was tested with PP disabled.

### Output consistency with PP=2 [Correctness]

This checks for requests resuming before all PP stages have loaded their KV.

- Qwen3-32B, PP=2, Mooncake Store, prefix caching off.
- `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, greedy decoding, 64 output tokens, to control for batching differences.
- Four runs: **off / on / on / off**, restarting vLLM and Mooncake and replaying the same seeded request schedule each time.
- Per run: 8 warm-up requests storing eight 8K-token prefixes, 171 requests reusing those prefixes, and 257 random-prompt background requests.

Results:
- **All 436 outputs matched across all four runs**, including warm-up.
- All 171 loads used early receive in each on run, and regular step outputs in each off run.

### TTFT with PP=1, 2, and 4 [Perf]

- One B300 node, Qwen3-32B, MRV2, async scheduling, standalone Mooncake Store over RDMA, prefix caching off.
- Hit requests: one of 16 stored 8K-token prefixes + 128 new tokens, 16 output tokens, Poisson arrivals at 2 req/s.
- Random-prompt background traffic kept the GPUs busy while loads completed; rates are listed below.
- 120 seconds per run, restarting both services and replaying the same seeded schedule. Each round paired an off run with an on run, reversing their order between rounds.

| PP | Background traffic | Off TTFT p50 / p90 (ms) | On TTFT p50 / p90 (ms) | Median paired change, 95% bootstrap CI (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1K tokens @ 4 req/s | 141.7–142.7 / 197.9–198.9 | 111.1–111.5 / 157.8–158.3 | −29.9 [−30.8, −28.7] |
| 2 | 1K tokens @ 4 req/s | 116.6–117.1 / 155.7–156.6 | 98.8–99.0 / 138.4–140.1 | −16.2 [−17.4, −15.4] |
| 4 | 2K tokens @ 6 req/s | 161.3–164.6 / 314.7–322.9 | 148.3–150.9 / 265.3–299.6 | −10.8 [−11.9, −9.7] |

Ranges are across rounds. Paired change is **on minus off for the same hit request within a round**, pooled across rounds. Per-round medians were −28.8 / −30.1 ms for PP=1, −16.0 / −16.2 ms for PP=2, and −12.2 / −8.3 / −11.4 ms for PP=4. Background traffic differs for PP=4, so comparisons are within each configuration.

Server timestamps showed the median delay from worker load completion to scheduler notification dropping from **33 / 21 / 16 ms to 4.6 / 3.9 / 5.4 ms** for PP=1 / 2 / 4. Time before load completion changed by about 1 ms or less, consistent with earlier reporting driving most of the TTFT improvement. Every hit in the on runs used early receive, with no material change in background ITL.

### TTFT with Llama-3.1-70B [Perf]

Same workload as above, with Llama-3.1-70B on four GPUs.

| Parallelism | Background traffic | Off TTFT p50 / p90 (ms) | On TTFT p50 / p90 (ms) | Median paired change, 95% bootstrap CI (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PP=4 | none | 151.3–151.4 / 184.8 | 128.5–130.0 / 156.4–158.6 | −12.9 [−17.5, −8.8] |
| PP=4 | 1K tokens @ 4 req/s | 183.0–185.2 / 292.9–303.6 | 142.0–145.9 / 276.6–280.7 | −26.0 [−27.2, −25.2] |
| TP=2 × PP=2 | 1K tokens @ 4 req/s | 153.3–153.6 / 216.6–218.3 | 133.4–133.8 / 193.2 | −16.6 [−17.5, −15.8] |

Per-round medians were −12.2 / −13.8 ms, −27.8 / −23.1 / −26.8 ms, and −17.9 / −15.4 ms for the three rows. The median delay from load completion to scheduler notification dropped from **27–28 / 34–35 / 22 ms to 2.3–3.0 / 6.5–7.4 / 5.8–5.9 ms**. Every hit in the on runs used early receive, and background ITL was unchanged in the runs with background traffic.

### Load-failure handling [Correctness]

This checks that failed loads stay on the normal reporting path and that the scheduler processes the failure before resuming the request.

- Stored prefixes: ~8K tokens of `item → six-digit code` entries; each request asks for one item's code.
- On the first load of roughly half the hits, selected Mooncake keys were renamed on chosen ranks to trigger real not-found errors.
- `kv_load_failure_policy="recompute"` unless noted.
- Background traffic: 2K-token prompts at 6 req/s.

| Configuration | Correct answers requiring recovery | Failures processed before request resumed |
|---|---|---|
| PP=4, failure on the last stage | 36/36 | 86/86 |
| PP=4, failure on stage 0 | 36/36 | 86/86 |
| PP=4, failure on all stages | 36/36 | 86/86 |
| TP=2 × PP=2, failure on all ranks | 36/36 | 86/86 |
| Hybrid Qwen3.8-27B, PP=4, failure on the last stage | 16/16 | 56/56 |

With `kv_load_failure_policy="fail"` at PP=4, all 86 affected requests returned an error, and every failure was processed before the request could resume.

As a negative control, suppressing failure reporting dropped accuracy to **10/36** in the PP=4 case and **1/16** in the hybrid case, confirming that these queries are sensitive to missing KV. Answers outside the failed chunks remained comparable to the run without injection.

### P/D with `MultiConnector` [Correctness]

This checks that the Mooncake Store and NIXL early paths work together in a real P/D deployment, and that a failed load on either side is processed before the request resumes.

- Prefill: Qwen3-32B, TP=4, `MultiConnector` with NixlConnector (producer) and MooncakeStoreConnector. Decode: TP=4, NixlConnector. Early receive on both.
- Prefill and decode on two nodes, transferring over RDMA; requests go through a proxy that runs prefill, then decode.
- Same fact-lookup prompts and background traffic as above.
- Prefill side: real Mooncake not-found errors, as above. Decode side: a NIXL pull is made to fail on all decode ranks or on rank 0 only, injected where the NIXL worker handles a failed transfer.

| Failure injected on | Correct answers requiring recovery | Failures processed before request resumed |
|---|---|---|
| none | 170/171 correct overall | — |
| prefill, Mooncake Store | 28/28 | 86/86 |
| decode, NIXL pull, all ranks | 86/86 | 86/86 |
| decode, NIXL pull, rank 0 only | 86/86 | 86/86 |

A follow-up on prefill performance: early receive helps more at larger chunked-prefill token budgets on a busy prefill instance.

Tested with Qwen3-32B, PP=4, and Mooncake Store. Cache-hit requests load an 8K-token prefix plus 128 new tokens at 2 req/s; background 4K-token prefills at 4 req/s keep the instance busy without saturating it.
| `--max-num-batched-tokens` | Step time p50 | Mean TTFT change | p90 TTFT change, 95% bootstrap CI |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2048 | 39 ms | −16 ms | −38 ms [−47, −27] |
| 8192 | 182 ms | −48 ms | −163 ms [−226, −116] |
| 16384 | 188 ms | −54 ms | −169 ms [−249, −77] |

At the larger budgets, p90 TTFT drops by about 17–20%, while the median barely moves. This is consistent with scheduling at step boundaries: most hits gain little, but an earlier completion signal can let some requests enter an earlier step and save roughly a full step.

8192 and 16384 perform similarly because fewer than 8K tokens are usually queued at this load, so their actual step times are nearly the same.

Hi, thanks for working on this!

I hit the same issue with **MooncakeStoreConnector + pipeline parallelism prefill**: when a KV load finishes, the scheduler only gets notified a few steps later, and the delay grows with the PP size. Your early-receive path fixes this nicely, and I've added Mooncake Store support on top of it with a small change:

- implement `has_pending_recving()` / `poll_finished_recving()` for MooncakeStoreConnector, so successful Mooncake Store loads are reported early;
- keep failed loads on the existing `get_finished()` path. They are not reported early, so the scheduler always sees the failure before it would run the request;
- drop the `PP == 1` check from the generic config validation. NIXL still rejects PP on its own, so nothing changes for NIXL.

Commit (on top of your latest head): [xsxszab/vllm@bba3ce6](https://github.com/xsxszab/vllm/commit/bba3ce6398)

---
**Setup:** Qwen3-32B on a single B300 node, TP=1, async scheduling, Mooncake Store over RDMA.

**Workload:** two kinds of requests run at the same time:

- **Measured requests** (2 req/s): each reuses an 8K-token prefix that is already stored in Mooncake, so vLLM loads that prefix from Mooncake and only computes the 128 new tokens.
- **Background requests:** random prompts with no shared prefix, so they never touch Mooncake. They only keep the GPUs busy. The "Background load" column below gives their prompt length and rate.

The table shows the TTFT of the measured requests only, with early receive off → on:

| PP | Background load | TTFT p50 | TTFT p90 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1K-token prompts, 4 req/s | 179 → 151 ms | 246 → 213 ms |
| 1 | 2K-token prompts, 6 req/s | 352 → 285 ms | 723 → 591 ms |
| 2 | 1K-token prompts, 4 req/s | 145 → 127 ms | 203 → 181 ms |
| 2 | 2K-token prompts, 6 req/s | 223 → 200 ms | 441 → 374 ms |
| 4 | 1K-token prompts, 4 req/s | 110 → 100 ms | 149 → 141 ms |
| 4 | 2K-token prompts, 6 req/s | 165 → 148 ms | 329 → 296 ms |
| 4 | 3K-token prompts, 6 req/s | 367 → 305 ms | 1242 → 941 ms |

Each row pools 2–3 runs per setting (~450 requests, ~200 for the last row). These numbers were measured on your earlier head (`47fb7e3`, before the switch to sleep-based waiting). I'm still re-running them on the current head and will post an update later.

---

One thing I noticed: the worker polling between RPCs matters a lot under heavy load. With it turned off, most of the gain was gone near saturation.

Related to that, polling may not be the best fit for every connector. Mooncake Store loads run in their own recv threads, which already know exactly when a load finishes, so they could push the notification right away instead of waiting for the worker to poll. An optional push-style hook (for example, a thread-safe notify function that a connector can call from its own thread) would keep the same benefit without the polling cost or the up-to-0.2 ms delay before the worker picks up the next RPC. I'm not asking to add it to this PR; I'm still trying to prototype it on my side to see if it works, just mention it here for completeness.

I can open this as a follow-up PR once this one is merged, and keep it rebased on your branch until then. If you'd rather have it land together with this PR, I can open a PR against your branch instead.

Small idea to simplify the worker loop: could we combine waiting for the next RPC with waiting for the next poll?

At the top of each iteration, run the poll if it is due; otherwise wait for an RPC, but only until the next poll is due. This replaces both `wait_for_poll()` and the post-step poll.

```python
rpc_mq = self.rpc_broadcast_mq
early_kv_recv = self.early_kv_recv

while True:
    if early_kv_recv is not None:
        timeout = early_kv_recv.time_until_poll()  # None: nothing to poll for
        if timeout is not None:
            if timeout <= 0:
                get_watch_dog().feed()
                early_kv_recv.poll()
                continue
            with get_watch_dog().disable():
                if not early_kv_recv.wait_for_rpc(rpc_mq, timeout):
                    continue

    with get_watch_dog().disable():
        rpc_request = rpc_mq.dequeue(indefinite=True)
    self._execute_worker_rpc(rpc_request)

    if early_kv_recv is not None and rpc_request[0] in (
        "execute_model",
        "sample_tokens",
    ):
        early_kv_recv.step_rpc_done()
    del rpc_request
```

This needs two new `EarlyKVRecvSender` methods in place of `wait_for_poll()`:

- `time_until_poll()` returns the seconds until `_next_poll`, or `None` when no poll is needed.
- `wait_for_rpc(rpc_mq, timeout)` spins on `rpc_mq.readable()` with `sched_yield()` for up to `timeout` seconds. It returns `True` once an RPC is ready or the queue is shutting down, and returns `False` when the poll is due.
- `step_rpc_done()` would also set `_next_poll = 0.0`, making the poll due at the top of the next iteration. This preserves immediate post-step polling without a separate call after the step or any assumption about the RPC duration.

Happy to prototype this and compare CPU usage and latency if the direction looks useful.

@xsxszab Thanks for the measurements and the Mooncake Store patch.

**Waiting:** you were right about spinning. The sleep came from our `85e8fef3f`, where we only compared CPU against the earlier spin; `MessageQueue.dequeue()` on main already spins with `sched_yield` for 1 s after each read, so the sleep saved CPU only relative to an idle worker and delayed RPCs that arrived during the wait by ~150 µs. `49c901449` spins on `readable()` with `sched_yield` until the next poll, like `dequeue()`. In a CPU-only probe with a no-op poll, an RPC that arrives while a pull is pending is now picked up 3–15 µs later than on main at p50, with the same CPU as main. A follow-up on prefill performance: early receive helps more at larger chunked-prefill token budgets on a busy prefill instance.

Tested with Qwen3-32B, PP=4, and Mooncake Store. Cache-hit requests load an 8K-token prefix plus 128 new tokens at 2 req/s; background 4K-token prefills at 4 req/s keep the instance busy without saturating it.
| `--max-num-batched-tokens` | Step time p50 | Mean TTFT change | p90 TTFT change, 95% bootstrap CI |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2048 | 39 ms | −16 ms | −38 ms [−47, −27] |
| 8192 | 182 ms | −48 ms | −163 ms [−226, −116] |
| 16384 | 188 ms | −54 ms | −169 ms [−249, −77] |

At the larger budgets, p90 TTFT drops by about 17–20%, while the median barely moves. This is consistent with scheduling at step boundaries: most hits gain little, but an earlier completion signal can let some requests enter an earlier step and save roughly a full step.

8192 and 16384 perform similarly because fewer than 8K tokens are usually queued at this load, so their actual step times are nearly the same.
